body.t: Hundreds of posts at farm scale: a spacing decision of one foot moves the order by dozens. Compute both spacings and price the difference.
One post per panel join plus one to finish — the straight-run rule this calculator applies so the last panel has something to meet.
Crowd barriers and site fencing are hired by the post-and-panel. A correct count is the difference between a tidy quote and a second delivery.
Replacing a storm-damaged run: count the bays, not the surviving posts — the spacing you inherit decides the number.
3,733.5 ft loop at 8 ft spacing: 3,733.5 ÷ 8 = 466.7, so 467 bays — and a closed loop needs exactly one post per bay, 467 posts. The loop closes on itself, so there is no extra end post.
A 100 ft garden run at 6 ft spacing: 100 ÷ 6 = 16.7, so 17 bays and 18 posts — bays plus one, because a straight run has two ends. This off-by-one is the entire reason the calculator exists.

faq: The number of posts a fence needs: length divided by spacing, rounded up to whole bays, plus the end post when the run is straight rather than a loop.
Yes — and it pairs with the Fence Length Calculator, which supplies the length this count consumes.
Exact arithmetic for the inputs given. Real fences add corner bracing, gate posts and spares — buy the count, then the extras your design names.
Why does a loop need fewer posts than a run?
A loop's last bay lands on the first post, so posts equal bays. A straight run's last bay lands on air, so it needs a final post: bays + 1.
By fence type: stock fencing commonly 8–12 ft with droppers between, post-and-rail shorter, garden panels fixed by panel width. The table shows what each choice costs in posts.
Corners and gateways take strain and usually get heavier posts and bracing — same count position, beefier item. The calculator counts positions; your design upgrades the corners.
What about a run with a gate in the middle?
Treat it as two straight runs meeting at gate posts — count each side as its own run and add the gate posts themselves.
What about intermediate droppers or stays?
Wire fences often add lightweight droppers between posts — they are counted per bay like posts but cost differently. This count is the structural posts; add droppers per bay if your design uses them.
How many spare posts should I buy?
A few percent for damage and mistakes is the usual practice — the count here is the fence's requirement, the spares are your judgement on top.
